records.old: 8 lessons × 40 minutes = 320 minutes total
records.new: 8 lessons (3 single lessons × 40 minutes + 5 double lessons × 80 minutes) = 520 minutes total
records.why: The unit total said 8 x 40 = 320 minutes, but Lessons 4 to 8 are double lessons of 80 minutes. Recomputed from the real lesson durations: Lessons 1-3 = 3 x 40 = 120; Lessons 4-8 = 5 x 80 = 400; 120 + 400 = 520 minutes (checked twice, by adding lesson by lesson: 40+40+40+80+80+80+80+80 = 520).

records.old: yet the mean, median and mode tell slightly different stories.
records.new: yet the different summaries tell slightly different stories (for travel mode only the mode can be found; for number data such as siblings or race times the mean, median and mode can differ).
records.reference: OpenStax Introductory Statistics (2e), Chapter 1 (qualitative versus quantitative data) and Chapter 2 (measures of the center apply to numerical data)
records.why: The phenomenon said the mean, median and mode of the travel data tell different stories, but travel mode is categories (Walk, Matatu...), so only the mode can be found; the lessons (3, 4, 7, 8) already teach exactly this. The anchoring phenomenon and puzzle are kept; only the explanation is corrected. Teacher to decide: whether you are happy with this wording of the puzzle. Checked by confirming that no lesson computes a mean or median of travel mode.

records.value:
• An Eldoret club coach must tell a selector how fast a group of seven 800 m runners is; one slow time (130 s, a runner with a cold) pulls the mean up, so the mean, median and mode tell different stories.
• A mandazi seller in Kisumu records daily sales for a week; a line graph shows a sharp rise on market day that the total alone hides.
• A newspaper pie chart of how a Nairobi family spends its monthly income (rent, food, school fees, transport, savings) leads to different conclusions depending on how the slices are read.
• The class tallies tree types in the school compound (grevillea, cypress, eucalyptus, neem) and the frequency table reveals which species dominates before anyone counts them again.
records.why: Two supporting phenomena did not match the lessons: the athlete example (two athletes, five races, Kericho team) is not what Lesson 4 uses (one Eldoret club group of seven runners with a 130 s outlier), and the tree list named jacaranda while Lesson 2 counts grevillea, cypress, eucalyptus and neem. They now match the lessons.

records.old: Mama Achieng's mandazi sold on 5 days are 40, 45, 42, 50 and 45.
records.new: Mama Achieng's mandazi sold on 5 days in an earlier, quieter week are 40, 45, 42, 50 and 45.
records.why: Lessons 4, 5 and 7 give Mama Achieng's Monday to Friday sales as 40, 45, 42, 50, 65, so the Lesson 3 numbers (Friday 45) contradicted them. Saying it is a different, quieter week removes the clash without changing any answer (222 / 5 = 44.4, mode 45).

records.old: learners rebuild the evidence pack from their own Lesson 2 to 7 work. (1) Tally the raw list (Learners 1-40) into a frequency table and check the frequencies add to 40:
records.new: learners assemble the evidence pack from their own Lesson 2 to 7 work, taking out the table, graphs and pie chart already made and redrawing only what is missing, so that this phase fits in about 22 minutes. (1) Use the frequency table from Lesson 2 (re-tally from the raw list only to settle a doubtful count) and check the frequencies add to 40:
records.why: Re-tallying 40 responses, redrawing a bar graph and a protractor pie chart, and working three more data sets from scratch would take far more than the 22 minutes available. Learners already made these in Lessons 2 to 7, so the project now asks them to retrieve and check them.

records.old: Learners then practise on new data: the 30 trees in the Lakeview compound
records.new: Learners then practise on new data as a take-home task (they begin it in class if time allows): the 30 trees in the Lakeview compound
records.group_headline: Lesson 2 could not fit 40 minutes; the 30-tree practice is now a take-home task instead of an in-class activity
records.why: Teacher to decide: the tree practice (6 minutes plus checking) cannot fit a 40-minute lesson that already tallies 40 responses and tests three claims, so I moved it to homework. Alternative: keep it in class and shorten the claims discussion, or carry it into Lesson 3, which is also full.

records.old: For the tree practice, supply the raw list of 30 responses and let pairs work independently for 6 minutes; cold-call 2 pairs to read their frequencies, and have the class check that the total is 30.
records.new: For the tree practice, hand out the raw list of 30 responses as a take-home task; learners swap tables with a neighbour when they hand them in, check that the total is 30, and you collect them.
records.why: Knock-on of moving the tree practice to homework: it is checked by neighbours when handed in rather than in a 6-minute in-class slot.

records.old: Remind them to use learner numbers, not names.
records.new: Remind them to use learner numbers, not names. Language support for English learners (teacher to confirm the terms with your Kiswahili department): write key words in both languages on the board, for example data = data/takwimu, table = jedwali, frequency = marudio, tally = alama za kuhesabu; let learners talk in Kiswahili first and then report in English.
records.group_headline: Added Kiswahili word supports for key statistics terms (suggested terms, to be confirmed by a Kiswahili teacher)
records.why: Teacher to decide: the lessons had no language support at all (guideline 12). I suggest commonly used Kiswahili terms, but I could not verify them, so please confirm or replace them with the terms your school uses.

records.old: Use the word 'mean', never 'average'.
records.new: Use the word 'mean', never 'average'. Language support (teacher to confirm): mean = wastani; for mode and median use the Kiswahili terms your department already teaches, and write each term with its meaning in both languages beside the formula.
records.why: Continues the Kiswahili support (see Lesson 2); terms to be confirmed by a Kiswahili teacher.

records.old: angles that sum to 359 or 361 because of rounding. Say: 'If your total is not 360, find the mistake before you draw.' Remind: 'Sharp points down, please.'
records.new: angles that do not sum to 360 (every angle here is a whole number, so a wrong total is a slip, not rounding). Say: 'If your total is not 360, find the mistake before you draw.' Remind: 'Sharp points down, please.' Support: if protractors are short, share one per group or use a printed circle with 40 equal tick marks (each learner is 9 degrees); give a cut-out 9-degree wedge to learners who find the protractor hard, and large-print squared paper to learners with low vision, who can also explain the finished chart aloud.
records.group_headline: Practical graph tasks had no fall-back for missing protractors, devices or learners who struggle; short, low-cost supports added to Lessons 5, 6 and 7
records.why: Protractors are often scarce in large classes and the task had no support for learners who struggle or have low vision. Also corrected the note that totals of 359 or 361 come from rounding: with n = 40 every angle is a whole number (checked: 126+108+36+27+27+36 = 360), so a wrong total can only be a slip.

records.old: Distribute squared paper, rulers and pencils (one set per group of 4).
records.new: Distribute squared paper, rulers and pencils (one set per group of 4). Support: give pre-printed axes to learners who find scales hard and large-print squared paper to learners with low vision.
records.why: Adds a short accommodation for the graph-drawing task (see Lesson 6 note).

records.old: Remind them: no internet needed.
records.new: Remind them: no internet needed. If no device is available, groups draw both versions on squared paper (one axis from 0, one from 2) and compare them.
records.why: Many partner schools do not have shared devices; without a paper fall-back the digital part could not be done and the 'change the axis' idea would be lost.

value.criterion: Organising data and calculating from tables
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: All percentages, angles, means and medians are correct, with clear working and the frequencies checked against the total.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Most calculations are correct with some working shown; one small slip in rounding or working.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Several calculations are incorrect or have no working; totals are not checked.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Chooses mean, median, mode and graph types correctly for each data type, and explains using the outlier and the categorical data.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Chooses most measures and graphs correctly with partial reasons.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Choices are unclear or not linked to the type of data.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses exact numbers (14 of 40, 35%; 12 of 40, 30%; 65%) to judge each claim, and correctly says the class count cannot test Zawadi's bus claim.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Judges the claims with some numbers; the bus claim is mentioned but not fully explained.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives opinions without numbers, or states the claims are right or wrong without evidence.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains the truncated axis effect (12 times against a true ratio of about 4.7) and lists several correct checks for an honest graph.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that the axis can mislead and lists some checks.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Does not recognise how a graph can mislead.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clear, honest report that links the steps from raw list to evidence, advises no shed, recommends whole-school data, and states the limit of one class.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives a clear recommendation but misses one step or the limit of the sample.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Recommendation is unclear or is not supported by the data.

records.why: The rubric used the generic words excellent / proficient / developing. The level names Exceeds / Meets / Approaches Expectations now start each descriptor so they match the CBE levels used in the lessons; the descriptors themselves are unchanged.

records.why: The contract allows only three rubric level fields, so the fourth CBE level, Below Expectations, cannot be represented in the Final Explanation. Suggestion: teachers treat work that does not reach Approaches Expectations as Below Expectations, or add that level by hand on the printed copy.

No KICD source for Essential Mathematics is available (the Grade 10 Mathematics PDF is the Core Mathematics design), so KICD wording could not be restored or checked. Differences from the Core text that look suspicious: Core 3.1 has six outcomes starting with 'collect data from real life sources', but this unit's outcomes a-e start at the frequency table, even though Lesson 1 cites 'collect data from the locality' as a KICD outcome; Core lists three key inquiry questions (What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?) but only the third appears here. Please check against the Essential Mathematics design.
